steps.body: Four building blocks of geometry. A **point** is an exact location — no size, just a spot, named with a capital letter. A **line** stretches forever in both directions. A **line segment** is a piece of a line with two definite endpoints. A **ray** starts at one point and shoots forever in a single direction.
Match the term to its description.

widget.prompt: Match each description to its geometric term.

left.label: Goes on forever in both directions
Starts at a point, goes forever one way

pairErrors.feedback: A line segment has TWO endpoints, going nowhere beyond them. A ray has just one endpoint and shoots off forever the other way.

widget.missFeedback: Count the endpoints: zero means a line, one means a ray, two means a segment.
widget.successFeedback: Zero endpoints is a line, one is a ray, two is a segment — the count tells them apart.

predict.prompt: What separates a LINE from a line SEGMENT?

options.label: A line runs forever both ways

predict.reveal: A segment has two endpoints and stops; a line refuses to end in either direction. 'Longer' is not the test — no finite length turns a segment into a line, and both are equally straight. The arrows in its drawing are a promise, not decoration.

explanationVariants: A flashlight beam starts at the flashlight and shoots forever in one direction — a ray.
One endpoint (the flashlight) and one direction of travel makes it a ray.

widget.prompt: A flashlight beam starts at the flashlight and travels straight ahead, seemingly forever. Which term fits best?

options.label: Ray — one endpoint, one direction
options.feedback: The flashlight is the one endpoint; the beam travels just one way — a ray.

options.label: Line — it goes on forever
options.feedback: A line has NO endpoints and goes both directions. The beam has one clear starting point — that makes it a ray.

options.label: Line segment — it has a clear start
options.feedback: A segment has TWO endpoints, stopping on both sides. The beam only stops at the flashlight — one endpoint means a ray.

options.label: Point — it starts at one spot
options.feedback: A point has no length at all. The beam clearly travels a distance — it's a ray, not a point.

steps.body: The endpoint count is the whole trick: **0 endpoints = line, 1 endpoint = ray, 2 endpoints = line segment.** Every shape's edge, every fence line, every beam of light fits one of these three.

explanationVariants: A fence between two posts has exactly two endpoints — a line segment.
Both posts mark definite stopping points.

widget.prompt: A fence runs between two fence posts, stopping at each one. What is this best described as?

options.label: A line segment — two endpoints
options.feedback: Both posts are definite stopping points — two endpoints means a line segment.

options.label: A line — it's straight
options.feedback: Straightness alone isn't the test — endpoint count is. This fence stops at both posts: two endpoints, a segment.

options.label: A ray — it starts somewhere
options.feedback: A ray has only ONE endpoint and keeps going. This fence stops at BOTH ends — two endpoints, a segment.

options.label: A point — posts mark exact spots
options.feedback: The posts are points, but the FENCE between them is the line segment — it has length, unlike a point.

widget.prompt: Sort each real-world example by how many endpoints it has.

items.label: A tightrope between two towers
items.feedback: Stops at both towers — two endpoints, a segment.

items.label: A sunbeam from the sun outward
items.feedback: Starts at the sun, travels one direction forever — one endpoint, a ray.

items.label: A ruler's printed edge, imagined stretching forever
items.feedback: Stretching forever both ways with no endpoints at all makes this a line.

items.label: A pencil lying on a desk, both ends visible
items.feedback: Both ends are visible stopping points — two endpoints, a segment.

widget.missFeedback: Count how many definite stopping points each example has.
widget.successFeedback: Tightropes and pencils have two endpoints; sunbeams have one; an endlessly stretching edge has none.

explanationVariants: An exact location with no size at all is a point.
A point marks a spot — it isn't a path with any length.

widget.prompt: A single dot marks an exact spot on a map, with no length or width. What term fits?

options.label: Point
options.feedback: An exact location with no size is a point — the simplest of the four terms.

options.label: Ray
options.feedback: A ray has length and travels forever in one direction. A dot with no length is a point.

options.label: Line segment
options.feedback: A segment has length between two endpoints. A dot with no length is a point.

options.label: Line
options.feedback: A line has infinite length. A dot marking just one spot is a point.

hints: A road connecting two named intersections has two definite stopping points.
Count the endpoints: the road stops at each intersection.
Two endpoints matches one specific term.
explanationVariants: A road stopping at two named intersections has exactly two endpoints — a line segment.
Both intersections mark definite stops, making it a segment, not a line or ray.

widget.prompt: On a city map, Main Street runs between First Avenue and Fifth Avenue, stopping at each. What term best describes this stretch of Main Street?

options.label: Line segment — it stops at both avenues
options.feedback: Two definite stopping points (the two avenues) make this a line segment.

options.label: Line — streets are usually straight
options.feedback: Straightness isn't the deciding factor — endpoints are. This street stops at BOTH ends: a segment.

options.label: Ray — it starts at First Avenue
options.feedback: A ray would keep going forever past Fifth Avenue. Since it stops there too, it's a segment, not a ray.

options.label: Point — intersections are exact spots
options.feedback: The intersections themselves are points, but the STREET between them has length — that makes it a segment.

takeaways: A point is an exact location with no size.
Lines have zero endpoints; rays have one; line segments have two.
Counting endpoints is the fast way to identify which term fits.
steps.teaser: next: what happens when two rays share a starting point.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Count the endpoints.** Zero means a line (endless both ways). One means a ray (endless one way). Two means a line segment (stops at both ends). A point has no length at all — just a spot.

explanationVariants: A pencil has two visible ends — two endpoints, a line segment.
Both ends of the pencil are definite stops.

widget.prompt: A pencil has two visible ends. What term fits?

options.label: Line segment
options.feedback: Two endpoints means a line segment.

options.label: Ray
options.feedback: A ray has only ONE endpoint. The pencil has two ends — a segment.

options.label: Line
options.feedback: A line has NO endpoints. The pencil clearly stops at both ends — a segment.
